language.script_notes: Street signs commonly read 'Straße', 'Weg', 'Platz', 'Allee', 'Ring', 'Gasse' — distinct vocabulary from Dutch/Austrian/Swiss German neighbours.

road_furniture.bollard_color: White, flat-profiled posts — flatter in cross-section than France's rounded bollards.
road_furniture.bollard_shape: Flat rectangular profile, distinct from the rounded posts common further west and south.
road_furniture.line_paint: White center/edge lines as the default; yellow lines temporarily mark construction zones (overriding the white lines underneath).
road_furniture.curb_style: Neat painted kerbs in towns; well-maintained road surfaces and shoulders nationwide.
road_furniture.km_marker_style: Standard German curve/chevron/roundabout/pedestrian sign designs. Aral, Esso, OMV, Total and Jet are common fuel-station brands. Deutsche Post's bright yellow branding appears frequently.

architecture.roof_style: Steep-pitched roofs nationwide as a rule, adapted for snow further south; half-hipped roofs common in the north and center.
architecture.roof_material: Terracotta/clay tile and slate widely used; red brick Gothic (Backstein) church and civic architecture concentrated in the north.
architecture.wall_construction: Half-timbered (Fachwerk) houses common across central Germany's old towns; brick Gothic construction in the north; Alpine timber chalet-style construction in the far south (Bavaria). See regional profiles for the north/south split.
architecture.wall_color_palette: Varies by region — see North/South profiles for specifics.
architecture.distinctive_building_types: Half-timbered (Fachwerk) old-town houses; brick Gothic churches and gabled townhouses in the north; Alpine chalet-style architecture with painted façades (Lüftlmalerei) in the south; onion-dome churches in Bavaria.

nature.vegetation: Beech and spruce forest widespread nationwide (the Black Forest, Bavarian Forest); flat marsh, heath and farmland across the North German Plain; vineyards along the Rhine/Mosel valleys.
nature.terrain: A flat northern plain rising into central uplands and forest, culminating in the Alps along the southern border with Austria; the Rhine, Elbe and Danube rivers cut through.
nature.climate_signature: Temperate, often overcast; snow-capped Alpine backdrop only in the far south; otherwise a fairly uniform green, well-ordered rural and forested look nationwide.

vehicles.plate_color: White plate, black text, blue EU strip on the left with a white 'D'.
vehicles.plate_format: 1-3 letter city/district code, then 1-2 letters and 1-4 digits (e.g. 'B-MW 1234' for Berlin) — single-letter codes (B, M, K, F, L, S) mark the largest cities.
vehicles.distinctive_vehicles: Overwhelming dominance of German-brand cars (VW, BMW, Mercedes, Audi) — a strong general tell versus most of the rest of the world.

google_coverage.camera_generation: Mostly Gen 4, very high quality and consistent across the country.
google_coverage.blur_style: Standard Google blurring, though Germany historically had more addresses opt out of Street View — some streets show pixelated/blurred entire building façades as a result.
google_coverage.coverage_notes: Dense and well-maintained coverage nationwide, including most rural roads.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Same German language, similar Alpine architecture in southern Germany/Bavaria specifically, similar road signage conventions
confusion_set.tiebreaker: German plates carry a city/district letter code system distinct from Austria's district codes; Bavaria's brighter Lüftlmalerei-painted façades and specific town styles differ subtly from Austrian equivalents, though this is a genuinely hard pair without other clues.

confusion_set.shared_traits: German-speaking cantons share the language and some Alpine architecture near the southern German border
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Swiss plates are white with a black canton code and no blue EU strip, unlike Germany's blue-strip 'D' plates; Switzerland is generally tidier with distinct road signage.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Flat northern terrain, similarly orderly infrastructure and cycling culture near the shared border
confusion_set.tiebreaker: German plates and vocabulary differ sharply from Dutch yellow-plate/Dutch-language signage; German 'Straße'/'Weg' vs. Dutch 'straat'/'weg' spelling and different plate colour scheme (Dutch plates are yellow).
